candidates.title: PRT bridge retires an epoch on a non-final ('latest') nonce check, so a shallow, within-policy reorg brings back that epoch's transaction as the journal's pending candidate. No bridge owns it any more, and every live epoch's bridge waits on it indefinitely, so no move of the live dispute is sent
candidates.component: PRT bridge and transaction journal in doc/recipes (prt-bridge.lua methods:tick, prt-transactions.lua methods:pending), run by crisium.lua pass()
candidates.role: Support (AUDIT.md: 'The PRT player and bridge in doc/recipes ... Support'). It stands in for the honest operator's transaction submission.
candidates.location: doc/recipes/prt-bridge.lua methods:tick lines 702-710 (the retirement check: '#jobs == 0 and settled' and transactions:pending() not of this epoch, then self.finished = settled block <= head(retirement_policy)) and lines 720-727 (an early return when the pending candidate's context.epoch ~= self.epoch: 'Another epoch's pending transaction is left alone until it is mined'). doc/recipes/prt-transactions.lua methods:pending lines 91-98 (reads the nonce at 'latest'; the record survives until forget_settled, which waits for finality). doc/recipes/crisium.lua pass() lines 318-331 (drops a finished listener and its bridge, then removes its files with --keep-epochs).
candidates.description: When an epoch's bridge has no jobs left and its settlement is irreversible, it retires. Its last guard asks the journal whether a candidate of this epoch is pending. transactions:pending() answers from the nonce at the 'latest' block, which is not final history: the journal keeps every nonce record up to high_water until a receipt sits at or below the finalized block. Suppose the epoch's own last transaction C (for example tryRecoveringBond or a cleanup such as eliminateMatchByTimeout, which anyone may send) was mined in a block above the 4-deep dispute observation head. Suppose also that the job disappeared from the snapshot for another reason: another party's identical permissionless call reached the observation head first. Dave's tryRecoveringBond turns later attempts into successful no-ops, so C does not even revert. The bridge then retires (self.finished), and crisium drops it. A shallow reorg of the blocks above the observation head is within both policies (dispute depth 4, input policy finalized or 8). Say it removes C's block and the node does not mine C again: the node drops it, or the base fee stays above C's max fee. The chain nonce then falls back to C's nonce, and transactions:pending() again returns C with context.epoch = X. Bridge X no longer exists. Bridge Y of the live epoch (sealed at X's acceptance, so it has joins and deadline-bound moves) reaches 'if candidate.context and candidate.context.epoch ~= tostring(self.epoch) then return snapshot, false, next_block end' at every tick. It never publishes, never replaces C and never cancels it. Nothing else in the process does either. With --keep-epochs=0, epoch X is not reopened after a relaunch either, because its checkpoint was removed when it retired. The wedge then also outlives restarts. With the default --keep-epochs=1, only a relaunch, which nothing triggers since nothing crashes, reopens X, and X then cancels C. The root cause is that the retirement decision acts on history that is not final, while the journal deliberately treats every nonce up to high_water as reopenable ('A reorg can resurrect every nonce up to high_water').
candidates.trigger: Three conditions together. (1) A permissionless action of an older epoch races another sender: the adversary, any validator, or the Dave node calls tryRecoveringBond, eliminateMatchByTimeout or eliminateInnerTournament ('Race and reorder transactions within the chain's rules', section 7). Its call reaches the dispute observation head while the honest player's own copy is mined above it. (2) Within the depth of the dispute policy, a reorg removes the block that holds the honest copy. (3) The node does not mine that transaction again: it drops it (a node that does not re-inject reorged transactions, or a pool flush) or keeps it underpriced (the base fee rises above its max fee, which an adversary can help by raising chain activity). Each condition is allowed: reorgs shallower than the input policy are not excluded by section 4.
candidates.reachability: Dave seals epoch X+1 at the acceptance of X, so the live epoch's joins and matches exist exactly when the older epoch's post-settlement jobs (bond recoveries, cleanups) are finishing. Bridge X retires at tip >= settlement + 8 (input policy 8, the demo default) or at finality. The honest copy only needs to sit within the top 4 blocks at that moment. The executed scenario shows the whole sequence with the real tick, attempt, cancel and journal code.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? The trigger is a reorg shallower than both policies, plus a permissionless race, plus a node that does not mine the reorged transaction again. Section 8 excludes 'Reorganizations of the chain deeper than the operator's input policy'; this one is shallower. Reading A (preferred): in scope. Section 4 says 'The honest operator acts only on history that its policy treats as final', and the bridge breaks this by retiring on the 'latest' nonce. Reading B: section 4 also says 'Acting on history before it is final, and recovering when that history is replaced, is outside this model'. A reviewer could read that as excluding the recovery from this reorg. The defect is that the component acts on non-final history at all; it is not about recovering after doing so legitimately. Condition (3) can be read as a host or node fault (node trusted, section 4). With the fee-rise variant, it is chain activity the adversary can raise (section 7).

2 Role: AUDIT.md puts 'The PRT player and bridge in doc/recipes' in Support. Section 3: 'A defect that only a support component shows is Medium when it would rate High or Critical in the role the component stands in for, such as ... the honest operator for an implementation of an operator'. In this case, the honest operator's transaction submission.

3 High/Medium cases: 'A defect that only a support component shows, when section 3 rates it Medium.' In the stood-in honest-operator role, the defect violates R4: 'The honest operator observes the chain and submits its transactions within the dispute clocks' and 'The honest operator defends every epoch whose dispute is open'. A7 adds: 'No rule of the referee may make the honest claim lose by timeout while it acts within its own clock.' The honest claim then loses by timeout. Step 4 would rate that Critical ('violating any rule ... anywhere on the honest operator's path is critical'), so the support defect is Medium.
4 Critical: not applicable to a support component (capped at Medium by step 2).

5 Low: Low under reading B or if condition (3) counts as a node fault. In that case the defect still violates the manual's journal promise that a reorg can resurrect nonces and the journal handles it.
candidates.claimed_severity: Medium (support standing in for a Critical R4 violation); Low under the reading that recovery from a replaced non-final history is outside the model
candidates.threat_to_goal: The goal assumes 'the chain includes its transactions within the dispute clocks'. Here the honest operator itself stops submitting for the live epoch: no join, bisection, seal or leaf proof is sent. If the honest claim is in a match, it loses by timeout, and 'If the honest claim is eliminated, a dishonest claim can win' (section 1, completeness failure). No error is reported, and crisium keeps passing, so the supervisor does not relaunch it.
candidates.evidence: Executed DYNBRIDGE/scenario-wedge.lua. It uses the real prt-transactions.lua journal (file-backed) and the real prt-bridge.lua tick, attempt and cancel; only observe, refresh, jobs and prepare are scripted. It runs against a scripted fake node (DYNBRIDGE/fakechain.lua: per-block nonce and state, base fee, a mempool with 10% replacement rules, reorgs, prt-rpc's own head/is_canonical/simulate/publish over an overridden rpc). Epoch 1 is settled at block 5. Its open-ended job e1-recover becomes due, and the honest copy is published at tip 13. Another party performs it in block 14 while the honest copy is underpriced, and the honest copy is mined in block 15. At tip 18 (head 14), crisium's pass drops the epoch 1 bridge as finished. A 4-block reorg replaces blocks 15-18; observation head 14 is untouched, finality is 12 deep. Output: 'after reorg tip 18 pending e1-recover@0'. Then 'tip 70: epoch-2 move [40,60) done=nil, pending=e1-recover@0' (exit 1). Variants: 'keep spike' (the node re-injects the transaction but the base fee is 5 gwei, above its 3 gwei max fee) also misses the move, exit 1. 'keep' (re-injected and mined) recovers, with the move done at 45. RESTART=keep0, a relaunch at tip 30 without epoch 1 (as --keep-epochs=0 leaves it), stays wedged, exit 1. RESTART=keep1, where epoch 1 is reopened, recovers: bridge 1 cancels its candidate. The random journal fuzzer did not reach the window by chance. Its jobs all end before settlement; the open-ended jobs of the 'retire' profile were raced too early.
candidates.test_idea: Build a deterministic Lua test: the real journal plus two real bridges, with observe/jobs/prepare stubbed, against an in-process fake node. Use the exact block script of scenario-wedge.lua: retire epoch 1 while its mined copy is above the observation head, reorg 4 blocks with the transaction dropped, then give epoch 2 a due move. Assert that epoch 2's move is published and mined within its window. Equivalently, assert that a bridge never reports finished while transactions:pending() could still return one of its own candidates after a within-policy reorg; checking at finality (forget_settled) is enough. Alternatively, assert that some live bridge cancels or replaces a pending candidate whose epoch has no bridge. Exits 1 today, 0 once retirement waits for the epoch's candidates to settle (or orphaned candidates are adopted).

candidates.title: PRT epoch listener aborts crisium ('epoch log history was truncated') when a within-policy reorg ends on a shorter branch under a numeric --input-policy (the demo's default 8): the observation head moves back over a still-canonical block whose input was already applied
candidates.component: PRT epoch listener in doc/recipes (prt-epoch.lua methods:poll with prt-log-history.lua observe/rewind), run by crisium.lua
candidates.role: Support (AUDIT.md: PRT player and bridge in doc/recipes). It stands in for the honest operator's chain observation and input delivery.
candidates.location: doc/recipes/prt-epoch.lua methods:poll line 30 (head = chain:head(input_policy), numeric policy = tip - depth), line 34 (history:observe), line 52 'assert(#logs >= #self.applied, "epoch log history was truncated")', lines 63-65 (positional applied check). doc/recipes/prt-log-history.lua observe() lines 54-59: rewind(self, math.min(common_ancestor(self), head)) drops the logs of blocks above the new, lower head even though they are canonical.
candidates.description: With a numeric input policy d, the observation head is tip - d. After a reorg that replaces only blocks above the previous observation head, the new branch can hold fewer blocks than the one it replaced; a fork-choice switch to a branch with missed slots does this. The tip number then decreases, and so does the head, even though no block at or below the old head changed. prt-log-history.observe(head) rewinds to min(old head, new head) and drops the logs of the blocks between them; they are refetched later when the head returns. prt-epoch.poll, however, compares the fresh, shorter log list with self.applied, the inputs already delivered to the player. It fails the assertion 'epoch log history was truncated', and the error propagates out of crisium's pass. The listener treats a lower observation head as a truncated history, although the history it applied is still canonical and final under its own policy. The same code then also refetches from scratch after the relaunch.
candidates.trigger: A chain reorganization whose fork point lies above the observation head (within the input policy) and whose new branch is shorter than the one it replaced. Also any node whose 'latest' number goes back by one or more blocks, such as a node behind a load balancer. No adversary action is needed beyond chain timing.
candidates.reachability: The default input policy of crisium is 'finalized', which never decreases. A numeric --input-policy is documented by crisium ('--input-policy=POLICY', rpc_client.policy accepts nonnegative depths) and is used by the recipe's own demo (prt-demo.lua: PRT_INPUT_CONFIRMATIONS default '8'). It needs at least one applied input in a block between the new and the old observation head.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? Section 8 excludes only 'Reorganizations of the chain deeper than the operator's input policy'; this reorg leaves every block at or below the old observation head canonical, so it is shallower than the policy. Not excluded. If the trigger is a node whose 'latest' goes backwards without a reorg, it is a node quirk (node trusted, section 4).
2 Role: Support (AUDIT.md). It stands in for the honest operator's chain observation.

3 High/Medium cases: 'A defect that only a support component shows, when section 3 rates it Medium.' In the honest-operator role the abort breaks 'The honest operator observes the chain and submits its transactions within the dispute clocks' (R4) only through the time a relaunch costs. R4 also says 'After a stop, it restarts ... and keeps defending its claim', and the relaunch does recover (shown). Reading A: a crash on a normal, within-policy chain event on the honest operator's path violates R4 and would be Critical in that role, so Medium for support. Reading B: the restart obligation is met and nothing is lost, so Low. The deciding fact is how long a relaunch of crisium plus the stored player takes relative to the clocks, and how often such reorgs occur.
candidates.claimed_severity: Low (preferred: the relaunch recovers); Medium under the reading that any within-policy chain event that stops the stood-in honest operator violates R4
candidates.threat_to_goal: The goal requires the honest operator to keep observing and responding within the clocks. Each such reorg kills the player process. The supervisor's relaunch reopens every epoch, refetches all logs and reloads the stored players, and each relaunch carries the O2 hazards already reported for reopening (R1-O2-1/2). Repeated short reorgs on chains that reorganize often (L2 unsafe heads, PoS late-block reorgs) multiply this downtime. No wrong hash results.
candidates.evidence: Executed DYNBRIDGE/scenario-listener.lua with the real prt-epoch.lua, prt-log-history.lua and prt-rpc.lua head/is_canonical/logs over the fake node. Inputs were in blocks 10, 11 and 12, with input policy 8. At tip 20 (head 12), 3 logs were applied. Then a reorg of depth 2 was replaced by 1 block (tip 19, head 11); block 12 is still canonical: true. Output: 'poll after reorg: ERROR: .../prt-epoch.lua:52: epoch log history was truncated' (exit 1). A fresh listener (what a relaunch builds) polls fine and delivers 2 inputs. Control: the same reorg depth with an equal-length branch: 'poll after reorg: ok'.
candidates.test_idea: Feed prt-epoch a scripted chain object (or anvil with anvil_reorg/evm_revert to a shorter branch above the observation head) under input_policy = 8. Apply an input in block head_old, then move the tip back by one block without replacing head_old. Assert that poll() does not raise and that, once the head returns, no input is lost or delivered twice. The test exits 1 today on the assertion at prt-epoch.lua:52.

candidates.title: crisium's WebSocket head subscription blocks without any timeout once a frame has started: a connection that stalls mid-frame (half-open TCP, stalled proxy) hangs the whole player forever, with no crash for prt-supervise.sh to relaunch
candidates.component: doc/recipes/prt-websocket.lua methods:receive / subscription_methods:wait, called from crisium.lua main loop (heads:wait(poll_interval)) when --ws is given
candidates.role: Support (AUDIT.md). It stands in for the honest operator's chain observation.
candidates.location: doc/recipes/prt-websocket.lua lines 78-109: after the first byte of a frame, 'self.tcp:settimeout(nil)' and blocking receives for the rest of the frame (comment: 'Once a message starts, the rest is read without a timeout'). doc/recipes/crisium.lua lines 359 and 375-380 (heads:wait(poll_interval) in the idle branch). No TCP keepalive is set on the socket.
candidates.description: wait(timeout) is meant to return within the poll interval so the loop reads the tip itself 'at least once per poll interval in case a header was missed'. However, once one byte of a frame has arrived, receive() switches the socket to no timeout and blocks until the frame completes or the connection errors. Without keepalive, a TCP connection that dies without FIN or RST never errors: a network partition, a NAT or load-balancer idle drop, or a proxy that stalls. crisium's single thread then stops observing, ticking and submitting for good. Because no error is raised, the supervisor never relaunches it. prt-rpc.lua, by contrast, bounds every HTTP exchange with a 60 s timeout.
candidates.trigger: A network fault between the player and its node, or a stalled WebSocket proxy, at the moment a newHeads frame is partly received. No adversary is involved.
candidates.reachability: --ws is an optional crisium option, and the recipe demo passes it. It happens whenever a stall falls inside a frame. New heads are pushed every block, so frames arrive constantly.
rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? The trigger is a host or network fault, or misbehaviour of the trusted node (section 4: 'the operator's host, keys, and node' are trusted; 'A host fault ... may stop the honest operator'). Under that reading it is out of scope. Counter-reading: the stop here is permanent and silent, not a stop followed by the restart that R4 expects ('After a stop, it restarts ... and keeps defending its claim').
2 Role: Support (AUDIT.md), standing in for the honest operator.
3 High/Medium cases: none fits directly. A stood-in honest-operator hang on a host fault is allowed by section 4, so it is not Critical in that role.
5 Low: a real robustness defect, a hang that defeats the supervisor, which violates no rule under the host-fault reading.
candidates.claimed_severity: Low (possibly out of scope as a host or network fault)
candidates.threat_to_goal: A silent, permanent wedge of the honest player, which keeps no deadline. It differs from a crash in that prt-supervise.sh cannot detect or recover from it.
candidates.evidence: Executed DYNBRIDGE/ws-stall.lua as a two-process test on 127.0.0.1, bounded by 'timeout'. The fake node completes the RFC 6455 handshake and the eth_subscribe reply, then sends one byte (0x81) of the next text frame and stays silent with the connection open. The client is the real prt-websocket new_head_subscription, then heads:wait(1), as crisium calls it. The client printed 'subscribed; calling heads:wait(1)', was still blocked 5.5 s later and was killed by timeout (exit 124). It returns only when the peer closes the socket (the server closed it after 8 s, which ends the wait with an error).
candidates.test_idea: Serve a WebSocket that sends a partial frame and then stalls. Assert that subscription:wait(1) returns, with nil or an error, within a bounded time such as 2 x timeout, or that crisium's loop reads the tip within its poll interval. The test exits 1 today: wait never returns while the peer keeps the connection open.

ran: Built a scripted fake EVM node (DYNBRIDGE/fakechain.lua). It has per-block state and nonces, an EIP-1559-style base fee, a one-account mempool with 10% replacement, 'nonce too low', 'already known' and 'nonce gap' errors, reorgs of depth <= 4 (equal, shorter or longer branches), re-injection or drop of reorged transactions, pool flushes, base-fee spikes, injected RPC failures (exceptions, as prt-rpc raises on HTTP and timeout failures), ambiguous publications (accepted, then failed), and kills right after the journal's durable store. Driven through prt-rpc's own head/is_canonical/simulate/publish. The journal fuzzer (DYNBRIDGE/journal-fuzz.lua) runs the REAL prt-transactions journal and the REAL prt-bridge tick, attempt and cancel, with 1-3 epochs sharing one signer and crisium-like passes (newest first, finished bridges dropped). Every injected crash is a process kill plus a relaunch from the on-disk journal. Valid seeded runs: clean 230, reorg 440, drop 240, fees 260, crash 240, all 500 (about 7,000 kills and relaunches), and retire 200 (open-ended jobs, permissionless races, reorg drops); about 2,100 runs in all, single-threaded, about 6 CPU-minutes. Checks per run: every job with a window of at least 12 blocks done exactly once on the final canonical chain, nothing pending at the end (no wedge), no error other than injected ones, and relaunches succeed. Result: no missed move, wedge, unexpected assert or duplicate success. The few misses traced to base-fee spikes above the --max-fee budget combined with crash bursts, or to harness bounds I then fixed. Reverted own moves were all re-inclusions of reorged transactions at a lower height; the journal recovered from each with one new nonce. Directed scenarios: scenario-wedge.lua (candidate 1, 5 variants), scenario-listener.lua (candidate 2, plus a control), and ws-stall.lua (candidate 3).
not_covered: No run against the local anvil with the pinned Dave contracts or the player-restart runner. Everything ran on the in-process fake node, whose mempool, replacement, base-fee and reorg semantics approximate geth or anvil (for example, base fee is set per block rather than derived from gas used, and only one sender is modelled).

The bridge's own observe() (prt-bridge.lua lines 48-204) under duplicate, out-of-order or removed logs and reorgs: it was replaced by a scripted snapshot in the journal fuzzer. Only prt-epoch's poll and prt-log-history ran for real against the fake node.

Fault injection at RPC sites other than through chain:rpc exceptions: malformed and oversized HTTP or JSON replies and chunked-encoding errors in prt-rpc.exchange were not fuzzed (node trusted by section 4). prt-log-history's page halving under provider limits was not exercised.

The insufficient-funds, out-of-gas (exhausted_gas doubling) and fee-ceiling 'held candidate' paths of prt-transactions were reached only incidentally. eth_estimateGas and eth_call non-revert error codes beyond those already reported (R5-INVBRIDGE-1/2) were not explored.
Power loss (page cache lost) rather than kill: the journal uses write_durable_file plus sync_directory, which I read but did not inject faults into (no device-mapper).

crisium end to end: the main loop's again/idle scheduling, open_epochs/get_seal under reorgs, remove_finished_epochs and checkpoint files across kills, and the stored player's reopen path after the candidate 2 crash.
Sentinel mode (methods:watch) and anomaly reporting under faults.

WebSocket faults other than a mid-frame stall: server close frames, fragmented messages, pings, and messages without params end crisium, as already noted in round 5. A subscription that silently stops pushing is covered by the poll-interval fallback. Not fuzzed.
